subtype: Expressing respect to teachers and mentors [Expressing]
passage:
Monday. Ira's project was accepted by the department, thanks to Pema, her mentor. Ira meant to say something but only mumbled "thanks, Ma'am" in the corridor. Pema smiled but was already rushing to class.

Wednesday. Ira wrote a short note: "Ma'am, your comment on my second draft, about linking the survey to the policy, changed my whole project. I'm grateful for the time you gave me." She left it on Pema's desk with a small pen.

Friday. Pema thanked her quietly after class and said the note had made her week. In the presentation, Ira credited Pema's guidance by name, and Pema nodded from the back.

qa.q: What did Ira leave with the note on Pema's desk?
qa.a: Ira left a small pen with the note.

qa.q: What was Ira feeling on Monday when she mumbled thanks?
qa.a: Ira felt grateful but couldn't say more in the rushed corridor, so she later wrote a note. The mumble did not show a lack of gratitude.

qa.q: What did Ira do that worked well to thank a mentor?
qa.a: She wrote a specific note naming the comment that mattered, and credited Pema by name in the presentation.

qa.q: How might Pema have felt about the note?
qa.a: Pema felt pleased, since she said it made her week, and the specific comment shows the mentoring was noticed.

grounding: A student thanks a mentor with a note, a small gift and a timely acknowledgement in a project.

subtype: Expressing respect to teachers and mentors [Expressing]
passage: Rukmini, you asked how we thanked teachers in my day. Kamal here. In my village school in Kerala, when Master Nair taught me algebra, we stood up when he entered and we'd bring him a few bananas at the end of the term, and I still remember his smile. When I went to a college abroad, my professor laughed when I stood up. "Sit, sit," she said. There, people just said "thank you, that helped." So I learned. I wrote her a short note saying which lecture had made things click. She kept it on her desk. Both ways were respectful. What matters is that they know you noticed.

qa.q: What did Kamal's class bring for Master Nair?
qa.a: They brought a few bananas.

qa.q: What did Kamal feel when the professor laughed at Kamal's standing up?
qa.a: Kamal was probably surprised and perhaps a little embarrassed, as the habit from home clashed with local custom. The professor's laugh seemed kind rather than mocking, so Kamal simply adapted.

qa.q: What could a student do when unsure how to thank a mentor?
qa.a: Watch local norms and write a short specific note about what helped.

qa.q: How might the professor have seen the note?
qa.a: The professor kept it on her desk, which suggests she valued the specific thanks.

grounding: An elder recalls that respect to teachers is shown by standing and gifts in one place and plain words in another.

subtype: Expressing respect to teachers and mentors [Expressing]
passage: It was Mridul sir's last day before retirement, and the college had given the farewell only fifteen minutes because of the rain. Swati had planned a speech, a card signed by thirty students, and a potted tulsi plant. Now the bus had been delayed, the hall was half empty, and she was soaked. She almost gave up. Then she saw him packing his books into a cloth bag. She walked up, put the wet plant on his desk and handed him the card. "Sir, you stayed after class for three months to explain thermodynamics to me until I understood. I passed because of you." Other students stood up, one by one, as they'd do in class when a teacher enters. Mridul sir looked at the card for a long time. "No speech?" he asked. "No time, sir." He smiled and patted the plant's leaves. "This is better than a speech."

qa.q: How long did the college give the farewell?
qa.a: Only fifteen minutes.

qa.q: What was Swati feeling when the bus was delayed and she arrived soaked?
qa.a: She was frustrated and discouraged, almost giving up on her planned speech and gifts.

qa.q: What worked in Swati's thank-you under pressure?
qa.a: She gave a short, specific acknowledgement of his help, with the card and plant, instead of the long planned speech.

qa.q: How did Mridul sir experience Swati's thanks?
qa.a: He was moved, looking at the card for a long time and saying it was better than a speech.

grounding: Shows a student thanking a mentor with specific words, a card and a small gift, alongside the formal gesture of standing.

subtype: Expressing respect to teachers and mentors [Expressing]
passage: In her small office at the Delhi university, Arohi ma'am was surprised when Devika knocked with a thick bound thesis and a small box of rasgullas. "Ma'am, I wanted you to see this first." Arohi opened it to the acknowledgements page. There, second line: "To Dr Arohi Sen, who read every draft, even the terrible one, and told me to keep the fieldwork chapter when I wanted to cut it." Devika shifted on her feet. She hadn't known whether to bring a gift; in her family, you never visit a teacher empty-handed, but a friend had said her supervisor found gifts awkward. So she'd chosen something small. Arohi read the line twice. "You remembered the terrible draft." "I remember everything you said about it," Devika said. Arohi laughed, put the rasgullas on the shelf and said, "I'll share these with the department. Thank you. This means a lot."

qa.q: What did Devika bring along with the thesis?
qa.a: A small box of rasgullas.

qa.q: What was Devika feeling as she stood in the office?
qa.a: She was a bit nervous, shifting on her feet, unsure whether the gift would feel right to Arohi ma'am.

qa.q: How did Devika handle not knowing the gift norms?
qa.a: She chose something small and let the thesis acknowledgement carry the main thanks, respecting both her family's habit and her supervisor's comfort.

qa.q: How did Arohi ma'am receive the thanks?
qa.a: She was touched, reading the line twice, and she shared the sweets with the department, which made the gift easy to accept.

grounding: Shows a student thanking a mentor through a timely acknowledgement in a project and a small gift, with norms that differ.

subtype: Expressing respect to teachers and mentors [Expressing]
passage:
"Are you touching Sharma sir's feet at the farewell?" Anjali asked, folding her dupatta.
Simran looked up from the card she was writing. "I wasn't planning to. Is that expected?"
"At my old college everyone did. It was how you showed respect."
"In my family we'd say thank you, maybe give a book. Touching feet is for grandparents."
"But he's from Varanasi. He might expect it."
"Or he might find it awkward. Remember Dr Mathews? She stepped back when someone tried."
Anjali bit her lip. "So what do we do?"
"Watch what the seniors do first," Simran said. "And whatever we do, say something real. Like how he let us redo the lab project."
At the farewell, a few seniors touched Sharma sir's feet; he blessed them warmly. Others shook his hand. Anjali bent to touch his feet; Simran gave her card and said, "Thank you for the second chance, sir." He smiled at both.

qa.q: What did Simran say to Sharma sir at the farewell?
qa.a: "Thank you for the second chance, sir."

qa.q: What was Anjali feeling before the farewell?
qa.a: She was unsure and a bit anxious, biting her lip, worried about getting the respect gesture wrong.

qa.q: What was wise about Simran's advice?
qa.a: Watching the seniors first and, whatever the gesture, saying something real and specific about what the teacher did.

qa.q: How did Sharma sir seem to see the different gestures?
qa.a: He smiled at both, suggesting he valued the respect behind touching feet and behind plain words equally.

grounding: Shows students choosing how to thank a teacher when norms differ, from touching feet to plain words.

subtype: Expressing respect to teachers and mentors [Expressing]
passage: I'm Lalremsiami, and at the end of my final-year project I didn't know how to thank Professor Mridul Bora. He had read four drafts, stayed late when our sensor failed, and never once made me feel stupid. On Teachers' Day some classmates had touched his feet and given him a shawl; he'd accepted with a slightly embarrassed smile. Back home in Aizawl we'd more likely cook for a teacher or bring a small gift, and touching feet isn't our custom; it didn't feel like mine to borrow. So I did two things. At the final presentation, on the first slide, I wrote, "Thanks to Prof. Mridul Bora, whose questions made this better." And I left a handwritten note on his desk saying which of his questions had changed my design. A week later he stopped me in the corridor. "That note," he said. "It's in my drawer." He looked more pleased than he had with the shawl.

qa.q: What did some classmates give the professor on Teachers' Day?
qa.a: A shawl, and they touched his feet.

qa.q: Why was Lalremsiami unsure how to thank the professor?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt deeply grateful but uncertain, since touching feet wasn't Lalremsiami's custom and borrowing it didn't feel genuine.

qa.q: Which forms of thanks suited Lalremsiami best?
qa.a: A public acknowledgement on the first slide and a handwritten note naming the question that changed the design: specific, timely and sincere.

qa.q: How did Professor Bora seem to receive the note?
qa.a: He was clearly touched, keeping it in his drawer and seeming more pleased than he had been with the shawl.

grounding: It illustrates a student thanking a mentor with a note and a timely acknowledgement, while showing that customs of respect such as touching feet or gifts differ.
